title: The durability of different anchoring points and anchoring types in the left ventricle in an ex vivo porcine model
authors: Henrik Bjursten; Per N Wierup; Sasha M. Koul; Matthias Götberg; Magnus Dencker
abstract: OBJECTIVE: Surgical mitral valve repair, including anchoring in different parts of the mitral apparatus, is the standard of care for severe mitral regurgitation. Various percutaneous approaches have been developed and are currently under development, but are struggling with durable results. This study investigates the durability of different anatomic anchoring points and anchoring types in the left ventricle. MATERIAL AND METHODS: Anchoring was tested with PTFE sutures or a 5 mm helix at three locations: the head of the papillary muscle, the lateral wall of the ventricle, and the apex of the ventricle. An accelerated life test was performed with 300 cycles at 3 N for each anchoring. Durability was assessed by measuring compliance (strain in mm until 3 N is reached), migration (change in strain from the first to the last cycle), and the occurrence of dehiscence. RESULTS: The lowest numerical strain/compliance in the first cycle was observed at the head of the papillary muscle anchoring (both surgical and helix). Migration of strain limits over 300 cycles was seen for all locations. The lowest migration was numerically for helix in the papillary muscle. CONCLUSION: PTFE in the head of the papillary muscle is standard practice in mitral valve repair and was used as a reference in the present study. The anchoring that yielded the most similar results was a helix in the papillary muscle, whereas other anchoring points showed greater compliance and/or migration.

title: Mitral Transcatheter Edge‐to‐Edge Repair at Centers With and Without On‐Site Cardiac Surgery: A Comparative Registry With a Shared Interventional Team
authors: Giulia Marchisio; Elisa Pelloni; Francesco Pisano; Lorenzo Zaccaro; Laura Contu; Maurizio B. Tusa; Nedy Brambilla; Marco Guerrini; Francesco Bedogni; Paolo Scacciatella
abstract: BACKGROUND: Comparative evidence for M-TEER performed at centers with versus without on-site cardiac surgery is lacking. We compared early outcomes at two centers that shared the same interventional operator team but differed in the availability of on-site cardiac surgery. METHODS: We retrospectively analyzed prospectively collected registry data from 64 consecutive patients with severe (4+) MR treated at a center without on-site cardiac surgery (no-CCH, n = 21) and a center with on-site cardiac surgery (CCH, n = 43). The same interventional operator team performed every procedure. At the no-CCH center, surgical expertise was provided through a shared Heart Team and a formal emergency transfer pathway. The cohorts were treated in sequential calendar periods. Principal comparative endpoints were MVARC device and procedural success at 30 days. Exploratory non-inferiority analyses used margins of -12.5% and -10%. RESULTS: MVARC technical success was 100% versus 97.7%. Device and procedural success were each 81.0% versus 72.1% (risk difference [RD] +8.9%, 95% CI -14.9 to +27.5; p = 0.547). Freedom from major MVARC serious adverse events was 95.2% versus 95.3%. Twelve of 16 device-success failures involved a mean transmitral gradient ≥ 5 mmHg. Surgical conversion and in-hospital death were 0% in both centers. CONCLUSIONS: In this preliminary same-team comparison, 30-day MVARC device and procedural success rates were 81.0% at the no-CCH center and 72.1% at the CCH center. Confidence intervals were wide and non-inferiority was not established. These findings support prospective evaluation of network-based M-TEER programs with shared interventional expertise and formal surgical backup.

title: Myocardial scar burden independently predicts response to cardiac resynchronization therapy
journal: International Journal of Drug Delivery Technology
abstract: Objectives: Cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT) has been shown to improve quality of life and reduce mortality in patients with heart failure.Around 30 -45% are non-responders to CRT.Determinants of response to CRT have been extensively studied.Faithful efforts were exerted to improve selection criteria for CRT beyond standard measures of electrical dyssynchrony.We aimed to assess the predictive value of amount and distribution of myocardial fibrosis to identify responders to CRT compared to conventional measures.Methodology: 58 patients who underwent CRT implantation on the basis of standard indication were studied.All patients had available myocardial imaging (cardiac MRI or nuclear scan) prior to CRT.Images were analyzed for scar quantification and distribution.Multiple variables were studied.Receiver operator characteristic (ROC) curve analysis was used to evaluate the ability of Global scar to predict response to CRT.Results: 30 patients of 58 were non-responders to CRT. 27 patients had non-ischemic cardiomyopathy, while 31 patients had ischemic cardiomyopathy.19 patients (70.3%) in the non-ischemic group, and 9 patients (32.2%) in the ischemic group were responders to CRT, with a statistically significant difference, p-value: 0.002.A cutoff threshold of myocardial scar at 22.9% independently predicted response to CRT with a sensitivity of 70% and a specificity of 92.9%.Conclusion: Global myocardial scar burden predicted response to CRT independent of etiology, regional distribution, and measures of electrical dyssynchrony.

title: Transjugular implantation of a leadless pacemaker in a 97-year-old patient with severe kyphosis and tortuous femoral veins: a case report
authors: Minghuan Fu; Xue-Fei Tao; Jie Gao; Yong Shi; Biao Cheng; Wei Zhang; Xiao-Han Chen
abstract: Background Leadless pacemaker systems offer significant benefits for frail older adults by avoiding pocket- and lead-related complications. However, anatomical challenges including severe spinal deformities and significant venous tortuosity can complicate conventional transfemoral or trans-subclavian implantation. Case report A 97-year-old man with severe kyphosis, tortuous femoral veins, and high-grade atrioventricular block was referred for permanent pacing. Supine positioning for subclavian access was not feasible, and the femoral anatomy posed an unacceptably high procedural risk. Following a multidisciplinary assessment and procedural planning, a transjugular approach was selected. Implantation was performed with the patient in the left lateral decubitus position, using adapted fluoroscopic projections and temporary femoral pacing as backup. An Aveir ventricular response leadless pacemaker was successfully delivered via the right internal jugular vein. Final device parameters were satisfactory, with a sensing amplitude of 8.5 mV, a pacing threshold of 0.5 V at 0.4 ms, and an impedance of 510 Ω. No perioperative complications occurred. At follow-up, exertional dyspnea had resolved, and device performance remained stable. Conclusion This case demonstrates that transjugular implantation of a leadless pacemaker can be a safe and feasible alternative for older adults with complex anatomical limitations that contraindicate standard pacing approaches. Careful preprocedural assessment and adaptation of intraoperative techniques are essential for procedural success in high-risk settings.

title: Residual Mitral Regurgitation After Surgical Mitral Valve Repair and Long-Term Recurrence and Reintervention
authors: JM Kong; Mingyang Yu; Jingxin Zhou
abstract: Surgical mitral valve repair is the preferred treatment for degenerative mitral regurgitation (MR) and is also widely performed for MR of other etiologies; however, recurrent MR after repair is not uncommon and is associated with adverse left ventricular remodeling and increased risks of mitral valve reintervention and death. At the completion of repair, a small amount of residual MR is frequently detected on intraoperative transesophageal echocardiography or predischarge transthoracic echocardiography, and whether mild residual MR is acceptable remains clinically controversial. Existing evidence derives largely from single-center studies with limited sample sizes, and the timing of residual MR assessment, grading thresholds, and outcome definitions vary considerably across studies, limiting the generalizability of their conclusions. We therefore plan to conduct a systematic review and meta-analysis. PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL) will be systematically searched for English-language studies of adults undergoing surgical mitral valve repair for MR of any etiology that report residual MR grade and long-term follow-up outcomes. The primary outcomes are recurrent MR (≥ moderate MR during follow-up) and mitral valve reintervention (surgical or transcatheter). In the primary analysis, adjusted hazard ratios will be pooled using random-effects models; unadjusted estimates will be pooled separately as supplementary analyses and will not be combined with adjusted estimates. Pooled estimates will be obtained separately for different residual MR thresholds (≥ mild vs. none/trace; > mild vs. ≤ mild). Subgroup analyses will be performed according to MR etiology (degenerative vs. other or mixed etiologies) and timing of residual MR assessment (intraoperative vs. early postoperative/predischarge vs. not specified), and the association of residual MR with long-term mortality will also be explored. Because death precludes subsequent reintervention, we will record whether included studies accounted for competing risks, and cause-specific and subdistribution hazard ratios will be pooled together in the primary analysis, with the measure type examined as a subgroup factor and a sensitivity analysis restricted to cause-specific hazard ratios. These analyses will be complemented by risk-of-bias assessment, sensitivity analyses (including recurrent MR defined as ≥ moderate-to-severe MR and reintervention restricted to surgical reoperation), and grading of the certainty of evidence. This study is expected to clarify the prognostic value of residual MR, particularly mild residual MR, thereby providing evidence to inform whether surgeons should aim for no or trace residual MR intraoperatively, whether a second pump run for re-repair is warranted, and how high-risk patients should be stratified for postoperative surveillance, as well as offering a reference for standardizing the definition and reporting of residual MR in future studies.

title: Von Willebrand Factor Biomarkers in Prosthetic Valve Dysfunction
authors: Sameed Arshad; Sabir Khan; Muhammad Zahid
abstract: Imaging remains the foundation of prosthetic valve surveillance because it identifies valve morphology, lesion mechanism, and hemodynamic severity. However, acoustic shadowing, eccentric or multiple regurgitant jets, loading conditions, and reader variability can complicate assessment, particularly for paravalvular regurgitation after transcatheter aortic valve replacement. High shear stress unfolds von Willebrand factor (VWF), promotes proteolysis of its high-molecular-weight multimers, and produces a measurable defect in primary hemostasis. Multimer analysis, closure time with adenosine diphosphate (CT-ADP), and the VWF activity-to-antigen ratio therefore provide a biologic signal of abnormal flow rather than an anatomic image. Prospective studies show that VWF abnormalities track residual paravalvular regurgitation during transcatheter aortic valve replacement, occur with dysfunctional prostheses, change after mitral paravalvular-leak repair, and are associated with bleeding. The evidence nevertheless remains observational; most diagnostic cohorts are small and single-center, thresholds lack independent validation, assays are vulnerable to hematologic and preanalytic confounding, and no completed randomized trial has shown that VWF-guided management improves outcomes. VWF testing is best viewed as an investigational adjunct when imaging and the clinical picture are discordant or when prosthetic dysfunction coexists with otherwise unexplained bleeding. It should not replace guideline-directed echocardiography or be used for routine surveillance outside research protocols.

title: Association between preoperative E/e′ and early left ventricular systolic recovery after coronary artery bypass grafting
authors: Jungsuk Choi; Hee Kyung Kim; Joon Kyu Kang
abstract: Background In patients with reduced or mildly reduced ejection fraction, the degree of systolic recovery after coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) is heterogeneous. We assessed whether routine preoperative transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) indices—particularly E/e′—are associated with early postoperative improvement in left ventricular function. Methods We retrospectively analyzed patients undergoing isolated CABG at a single tertiary center (April 2019 to July 2025). Eligibility required a preoperative left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) of <50%. Emergency/salvage operations, 30-day deaths, and patients without an evaluable early postoperative TTE were excluded. The primary outcome was an absolute increase in the LVEF of ≥10 percentage points. Because of the limited number of outcome events, the primary association analysis used a single-predictor logistic regression model with preoperative E/e′. Sensitivity analyses excluded patients with preoperative atrial fibrillation (AF) and modeled postoperative LVEF as a continuous outcome adjusted for baseline LVEF. Results Of 75 otherwise clinically eligible patients, three lacked an evaluable early postoperative TTE, leaving 72 patients for outcome analysis; 17 (23.6%) achieved an LVEF increase of ≥10 percentage points. A higher preoperative E/e′ was associated with early LVEF improvement (OR 1.155 per 1-unit increase; 95% CI 1.04–1.28; p = 0.005; N = 66; 16 events). The apparent AUC was 0.700; after 1,000-resample bootstrap internal validation, the estimated optimism was 0.004 and the optimism-corrected AUC was 0.696 (95% bootstrap CI 0.526–0.885). The association persisted after excluding patients with AF (OR 1.14; 95% CI 1.02–1.27; p = 0.025). In a sensitivity analysis using postoperative LVEF as a continuous outcome, E/e′ remained associated with postoperative LVEF after adjustment for baseline LVEF ( β = 0.31 percentage points per 1-unit increase; 95% CI 0.01–0.61; p = 0.042). Conclusion A higher preoperative E/e′ was associated with early improvement in LV systolic function after CABG among patients with a preoperative LVEF of <50% who survived to undergo early postoperative echocardiographic assessment. Given the small number of events and the single-center retrospective design, these findings are hypothesis-generating and require external validation.

title: Morphometric Study of the Mitral and Tricuspid Annuli in Fresh Cadaveric Human Hearts From Uttar Pradesh, India
authors: Keerthy L K; Jyoti Chopra; Anurag Rai; Anita Rani; Anoop Verma; Heena Singh
abstract: Background: Accurate knowledge of mitral and tricuspid annular morphometry is fundamental to the planning of valve repair, annuloplasty, and transcatheter interventions.Population-and ethnicity-specific reference data remain limited for fresh human hearts in Uttar Pradesh.Objective: This study aims to determine the anteroposterior and transverse diameters of the mitral and tricuspid valve annuli in fresh human cadaveric hearts of the North Indian population and to compare these findings with existing anatomical and echocardiographic literature.Methods: This cross-sectional analytical study was conducted on 100 fresh human cadaveric hearts.The right atrium and left atrium were opened along standard anatomical planes to expose the tricuspid and mitral annuli, respectively.The anteroposterior and transverse diameters of both annuli were measured using a digital vernier caliper.Results: The mean anteroposterior and transverse annular diameters of the mitral valve were 2.7 ± 0.4 cm and 2.9 ± 0.3 cm, respectively.The mean anteroposterior and transverse annular diameters of the tricuspid valve were 3.1 ± 0.3 cm and 3.3 ± 0.4 cm, respectively.the mean area of the mitral valve orifice was 6.19 ± 1.34 cm², while that of the tricuspid valve orifice was 8.07 ± 1.70 cm².Conclusion: This study provides descriptive anatomical reference data for mitral and tricuspid annular dimensions in fresh human cadaveric hearts from the Uttar Pradesh population.

title: Circulating microRNAs as potential candidate biomarkers of left ventricular reverse remodeling after myocardial infarction: A pilot study
authors: Roksana Gozdowska; Marcin Antoni Konopka; Anna Hojka-Osińska; Grzegorz Jas; Katarzyna Czarzasta; Agnieszka Cudnoch‐Jędrzejewska; Wojciech Braksator; Dominika Klimczak‐Tomaniak; Marek Kuch
abstract: BACKGROUND: Myocardial infarction (MI) induces cardiac remodeling and lead to heart failure. Some patients experience reverse remodeling, characterized by improved LV function. MicroRNAs (miRNAs) regulate gene expression and play a crucial role in remodeling processes. OBJECTIVES: We aimed to investigate the role of miRNAs in cardiac reverse remodeling after MI and identify candidate miRNAs that could predict better response to cardiac rehabilitation. METHODS: The study enrolled 39 patients following their first MI. For final analysis, 10 patients meeting echocardiographic criteria for LVRR at 8-week follow-up (absolute LVEF increase ≥ 10% or LVESV reduction ≥ 15%) were matched with 10 patients with stable LV status (SLVS). All patients completed a cardiac rehabilitation program. Expression of 375 circulating miRNAs was quantified - those with higher baseline accumulation in the LVRR group were identified as candidate biomarkers and their target genes were analyzed. RESULTS: Twenty patients (mean age 57 ± 9 years) were analyzed. At baseline, the SLVS group exhibited significantly higher LVEF compared to the LVRR group (53% vs. 44%, p = 0.013). Baseline regional contractility impairment in all LVRR patients was reversed in 70% of them at follow-up. Fourteen miRNAs (-15b-5p, -24-3p, -29c-3p, -99b-5p, -127-3p, -146a-5p, -199a-3p, -361-5p, -502-5p, -625-5p, -376c-3p, -18b-5p, -342-5p, and -429) were identified as candidate LVRR biomarkers. Enrichment analysis linked their targets to PI3K-Akt, MAPK, FoxO, and HIF-1 pathways. CONCLUSIONS: This study identifies 14 candidate miRNAs as LVRR biomarkers post-MI. These findings highlight the biological relevance of non-coding RNA and support the need for further research and validation in large, non-pooled cohorts. UNSTRUCTURED ABSTRACT: Myocardial infarction triggers adverse cardiac remodeling, though some patients achieve left ventricular reverse remodeling (LVRR), marked by functional and structural recovery. This pilot study investigated 39 patients to identify circulating microRNAs (miRNAs) that predict positive responses to cardiac rehabilitation. Comparing 10 LVRR responders against 10 stable patients, we quantified 375 miRNAs via RT-qPCR. At baseline, the stable group had higher ejection fractions (53% vs. 44%, p = 0.013), but 70% of LVRR patients reversed regional contractility impairment by the 8-week follow-up. We identified 14 potential biomarkers, including novel candidates (miR-502-5p, miR-376c-3p, and miR-18b-5p), whose target genes enrich pathways like PI3K-Akt, MAPK, and FoxO. These findings bridge the gap between preclinical data and clinical settings, highlighting the therapeutic potential of non-coding RNAs in cardiac reverse remodeling and necessitating further validation in larger cohorts.

title: Marfan Syndrome: A Case Report
authors: Abdullah Al Saleh
journal: International Journal of Science and Research (IJSR)
abstract: Marfan syndrome is an autosomal dominant systemic disorder of the connective tissue. Children affected by the Marfan syndrome carry a mutation in one of their two copies of the gene that encodes the connective tissue protein fibrillin-1. Marfan syndrome affects most organs and tissues, especially the skeleton, lungs, eyes, heart, and the large blood vessel that distributes blood from the heart to the rest of the body. I will report a case of Marfan syndrome which was incidentally diagnosed in a 9-year-old male presenting with anorexia after routine physical examination revealed positive Steinberg (thumb) and Walker-Murdoch (wrist) signs. Subsequent diagnostic workup confirmed aortic root dilation (Z-score +2.8) and bilateral ectopia lentis. The Revised Ghent Nosology criteria alongside a confirmed FBN1 gene mutation. This case report highlights the clinical utility of physical examination during routine pediatric evaluations.

title: Clinical manifestations of resistance to thyroid hormone beta (RTHβ) syndrome in children – multicenter case series
authors: Anna Fedorczak; Martyna Sokół; Iwona Beń‐Skowronek; Magdalena Mierzwa; Agnieszka Zachurzok; Agnieszka Bogusz-Wójcik; Julia Przybylak-Ortega; Elżbieta Moszczyńska; Paulina Berezowiec; Artur Bossowski; Natalia Dąbek; Artur Mazur; Kamil Dyrka; Marek Niedziela; Magdalena Makowiecka-Wolek; Robert Stanisław Śmigiel; Agnieszka Ulenberg; Małgorzata Myśliwiec; Renata Stawerska
abstract: Introduction Resistance to thyroid hormone (TH) β (RTHβ) is a rare genetic disorder caused by mutations in the TH receptor β gene ( THRB ) and characterized by elevated TH levels with non-suppressed thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) and variable clinical presentation. The aim of the study was to characterize the clinical and biochemical features of children with RTHβ, correlate them with genetic findings and therapeutic management, to raise clinicians’ awareness of the specific characteristics of the condition. Material and methods This retrospective multicenter case series included 15 children with genetically confirmed THRB variants. Clinical, laboratory, imaging, and treatment data were analyzed retrospectively. Results All the patients demonstrated elevated free thyroxine and free triiodothyronine concentrations with detectable, non-suppressed TSH serum level. Common findings included tachycardia (73%), neurodevelopmental disturbances (60%), and a lean phenotype (BMI <10th percentile, 53%). Misdiagnosis of primary hyperthyroidism occurred in 20% of cases. Most patients did not require pharmacological treatment or were managed with beta-blockers alone for symptomatic tachycardia control. Discussion Pediatric RTHβ shows consistent biochemical features but marked clinical heterogeneity. Awareness is essential to ensure accurate diagnosis and avoid unnecessary therapy.

title: Right internal jugular approach for transcatheter edge-to-edge mitral valve repair using the MitraClip G4 system after failed transfemoral access: a case report
authors: Yutaka Konami; Kazuhisa Kodama; Mika Maeda; Masahiro Yamada; Tomohiro Sakamoto
abstract: Abstract Background Transcatheter edge-to-edge repair of the mitral valve is conventionally performed via transfemoral venous access. When this route is not feasible, the right internal jugular vein may provide an alternative, but procedural experience remains limited. Case Summary A 93-year-old woman with refractory heart failure had atrial functional mitral regurgitation and low-flow, low-gradient aortic stenosis. After transcatheter aortic valve implantation, moderate-to-severe mitral regurgitation persisted. Transfemoral edge-to-edge repair was unsuccessful because severe iliac venous tortuosity prevented adequate catheter control. The procedure was subsequently performed via the right internal jugular vein using the MitraClip G4 system. A pre-existing iatrogenic atrial septal defect was reused, and temporary left ventricular apical wire support facilitated advancement of the steerable guiding catheter into the left atrium. Stepwise + knob rotation increased height and working space, improved the markedly under-straddled configuration, and permitted further advancement of the clip delivery system. Subsequent M- and P-knob adjustments achieved an appropriate trajectory towards A2/P2, with an S-shaped fluoroscopic configuration. Leaflet grasping reduced mitral regurgitation to mild without access-site complications. Mild mitral regurgitation was maintained at 6 months without heart-failure rehospitalization. Discussion Right internal jugular access may be a feasible alternative when transfemoral access is not possible. Successful navigation requires recognition of access-specific catheter behaviour and adaptation of steering under real-time fluoroscopy and transoesophageal echocardiography. An S-shaped fluoroscopic configuration may serve as a practical landmark of a favourable trajectory towards the mitral valve.

title: Multidimensional Echocardiographic Parameters Predict Left Ventricular Functional Recovery After Coronary Artery Bypass Grafting
authors: Man Zhang; Jun Xia; Xiaoling Wan; Xuejiao Chen
abstract: AIM: This study aimed to investigate the predictive value of preoperative and early postoperative echocardiographic parameters for left ventricular function recovery after coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG), and to evaluate the relationship between functional recovery and 1-year clinical prognosis.METHODS: This retrospective cohort included 214 patients undergoing first-time elective CABG at The First Affiliated Hospital of Yangtze University between January 2022 and October 2024. Transthoracic echocardiography was performed preoperatively, 3–7 days postoperatively, and at 6 months to evaluate left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF), global longitudinal strain (GLS), left atrial volume index (LAVI), and ratio of early mitral inflow velocity to early diastolic mitral annular velocity (E/e′). Based on 6‑month LVEF change, patients were divided into recovery (ΔLVEF ≥5%) and non‑recovery (ΔLVEF <5%) groups. Multivariate logistic regression was used to identify independent predictors, and the corresponding models were established and validated. Major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) were recorded at 1‑year follow‑up.RESULTS: Of the 214 patients enrolled in the study, functional recovery of the left ventricle was observed in 128 individuals, corresponding to 59.8% of the cohort. Multivariate analysis identified several preoperative and procedural variables as independent predictors of functional recovery, including left atrial volume index (LAVI), left ventricular end-diastolic diameter (LVEDD), left ventricular end-systolic diameter (LVESD), left atrial diameter (LAD), Synergy between Percutaneous Coronary Intervention with TAXUS and Cardiac Surgery (SYNTAX) score, and the number of graft vessels. Age, preoperative LVEF, and e′ velocity were independently associated with lower odds of functional recovery. Global longitudinal strain (GLS) and diabetes history showed no independent predictive value. The clinical-echocardiographic combined model demonstrated excellent discrimination and showed higher discriminative performance than the basic clinical model and conventional echocardiographic model. Subgroup analysis revealed that GLS showed no independent predictive value across all LVEF subgroups (p > 0.05), whereas LAVI and LAD were significant predictors in patients with LVEF ≥40% (including the 40%–49% subgroup), but showed no predictive relevance in those with LVEF <40%. Early postoperative ΔLVEF predicted 6-month functional recovery with an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.846. After one year of follow‑up, the recovery group exhibited a markedly lower rate of MACE than the non‑recovery group, with left ventricular functional recovery serving as an independent protective factor against MACE.CONCLUSIONS: Preoperative structural parameters, including LAVI, LVEDD, LVESD, and LAD, are independent imaging biomarkers for predicting left ventricular functional recovery after CABG. GLS and E/e′ ratio show no independent predictive value in this study. The integrated model combining clinical factors with multi-dimensional echocardiographic parameters demonstrates excellent discriminative ability. Early postoperative LVEF improvement strongly predicts 6-month functional recovery, while postoperative recovery of left ventricular function is associated with a significantly lower 1-year MACE risk.

title: External validation of the D-PACE score for predicting late high-grade atrioventricular block after transcatheter aortic valve replacement in a Colombian cohort
authors: Juan David Zuluaga-Monroy; Hugo Oswaldo Alvarado Mora; Diana Fernanda Bohorquez Gonzalez; J.J. Sierra; Edgar Fernando Hurtado Ordoñez
abstract: Background Transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) carries a clinically significant risk of late high-grade atrioventricular block (AVB), yet no validated tool exists to predict this complication in Latin-American populations. The D-PACE score was developed in European cohorts for this purpose. Methods In a retrospective cohort of 175 consecutive TAVR procedures at a Colombian center (2012–2025), 141 patients met inclusion criteria for D-PACE validation. The primary outcome was late high-grade AVB (≥Mobitz type II) occurring between 24 h and 30 days post-TAVR. Discrimination, logistic-regression calibration, and decision curve analysis were performed. Results Late AVB occurred in 31 patients (22.0%), with 80.6% of events within 72 h. The D-PACE score demonstrated good discrimination (AUC 0.82; 95% CI 0.71–0.92; sensitivity 77.4%, specificity 86.4% at a cutoff of 5.5 points; NPV 93.1%). Late AVB rates rose progressively across strata: 5.9% (low-risk, score 0–3), 8.8% (intermediate, 4–5), and 61.5% (high-risk, ≥6), with the high-risk group concentrating 77.4% of all events. Decision curve analysis confirmed net clinical benefit across threshold probabilities from 8% to 60%. All four low-risk events occurred among valve-in-valve patients assigned a score of 0 per the original algorithm; excluding this subgroup ( N = 114), the AUC rose to 0.91 (95% CI 0.85–0.96) with zero low-risk events. In an exploratory analysis applying the full seven-variable scoring uniformly, including valve-in-valve cases, the AUC was 0.90 (95% CI 0.85–0.95; NPV 96.7%), and 0.91 (95% CI 0.78–1.00) within the valve-in-valve subgroup ( N = 27, 4 events). Conclusions Applied as originally specified, the D-PACE score showed good discrimination for late high-grade AVB in this cohort (AUC 0.82; 95% CI 0.71–0.92). The algorithm's automatic low-risk classification of valve-in-valve patients was not supported (14.8% AVB rate). Discrimination was higher both in the sensitivity analysis excluding valve-in-valve cases and in the exploratory analysis applying the seven-variable scoring uniformly, indicating that the scoring variables transfer well while the valve-in-valve exemption warrants reconsideration. These findings provide the first external validation of D-PACE in Latin America.

title: Vasospastic Angina and Cardiac Arrest
authors: Kazuya Tateishi; Yuichi Saito; Ken Kato; Hideki Kitahara; Yoshio Kobayashi
abstract: Vasospastic angina (VSA) is an important and potentially treatable cause of cardiac arrest (CA) and may account for approximately 2–10% of otherwise unexplained cases of out-of-hospital CA. VSA can sometimes be diagnosed by spontaneous coronary spasm during emergency coronary angiography or by transient ST-segment elevation during a spontaneous attack after resuscitation. However, because coronary spasm is transient and may not be evident during the initial evaluation, provocation testing after clinical stabilization may be required to establish the diagnosis in otherwise unexplained cases. Once VSA is diagnosed, vasodilator therapy, particularly calcium-channel blockers, is the mainstay of treatment. Nevertheless, survivors of VSA-related CA may remain at risk of recurrent lethal ventricular arrhythmias despite medical therapy. Evaluation for alternative or overlapping arrhythmogenic disorders, including cardiomyopathies and channelopathies, should therefore be considered even after a diagnosis of VSA, and implantable cardioverter-defibrillator implantation may be considered in selected patients according to the risk of recurrence and response to medical therapy. Further prospective studies, including randomized controlled trials, are needed to determine whether systematic provocation testing followed by targeted therapy reduces recurrent ventricular arrhythmias and CA and improves long-term outcomes.

title: Beyond the clinic: a six-month home-based exercise and respiratory rehabilitation program improves functional capacity, respiratory muscle strength, and fatigue in chronic heart failure
authors: Mariusz Ciołkiewicz; Mariusz Wojciuk; Anna Kuryliszyn-Moskal; Agnieszka Dakowicz; Emilia Sawicka; Karol Adam Kamiński
abstract: Introduction Optimal models of rehabilitation dedicated for patients with heart failure (HF) remain under investigation. The aim of this study was to assess the safety and effectiveness of a 6-month home-based rehabilitation program in patients with HF. Materials and methods 63 patients with stable HF were randomized, 28 patients from intervention group completed the study and were included in the analysis. Assessments including the 6-minute walk test, respiratory muscle strength, and quality of life measures (SF-36 and Fatigue Severity Scale – FSS) were conducted at baseline and after 6 months. Additionally, adverse events and adherence to the training protocol were monitored. Results Due to objective challenges caused by the COVID-19 pandemic outbreak, the course and final outcomes of the study differed from the original protocol; the control group was not assessed after 6 months. In the intervention group, 6 months of rehabilitation resulted in statistically significant improvements: the 6-minute walk distance increased by 37.86 meters ( p = 0.001), maximal inspiratory pressure (PImax) improved by 20.21 cmH₂O, and maximal expiratory pressure (PEmax) by 20.75 cmH₂O (both p < 0.01). A significant reduction in fatigue was observed, as measured by FSS, with a mean decrease of 0.68 points ( p = 0.029). Adherence to the exercise protocol averaged 91.5 ± 15.3%. No serious adverse events were reported. Conclusions The home-based rehabilitation program, including respiratory muscle training, is safe and effective for patients with chronic HF. It improves functional capacity and reduces fatigue levels. Clinical Trial registration https://clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT03780803 , ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT03780803. Registered 19/12/2018.

title: Antecedents and consequences of Green-tech FDI in emerging markets
authors: Zhuoran Liu
abstract: As environmental pressures intensify, attracting sustainable foreign direct investment (FDI), particularly green-tech FDI, has become a critical pathway for emerging markets to achieve environmental sustainability. However, existing research remains fragmented, offering limited insights into why green-tech FDI enters emerging markets and how it affects regional green innovation. This thesis addresses these gaps by systematically examining both the antecedents and consequences of green-tech FDI through three empirical studies using regional data from China. Study 1 and Study 2 focus on the antecedents of green-tech FDI. Study 1 examines how host-country conditions can attract green-tech FDI, highlighting the role of environmental management information disclosure (EMID) by domestic firms in reducing information gaps and strengthening green market–seeking motives. Study 2 shifts attention to the active decision-making of green-tech FDI, showing that under uncertainty, green-tech foreign investors engage in identity-based bandwagon learning by imitating peers with similar green identities, thereby mitigating investment risks. Study 3 turns to the consequences of green-tech FDI. It demonstrates that, due to the technological complexity of green innovation and limited absorptive capacity in emerging markets, green-tech FDI may generate crowding-out effects rather than purely positive spillovers. Adopting a network perspective, the study further finds that universities play a key moderating role: through broad linkages and deep collaborations, they help mitigate negative spillovers and facilitate the diffusion of green technologies. Together, the three studies advance the literature on sustainable FDI by differentiating green-tech FDI from general FDI and identifying the specific mechanisms that shape its entry decisions and local innovation outcomes. Practically, the findings provide guidance for emerging-market governments and firms on how to attract and manage sustainable investment, balance growth with environmental objectives, and strengthen local innovation ecosystems.

title: Combating Data and Target Shifts in Visual Tasks
authors: Zhaorui Tan
abstract: The rapid advancement of deep learning models for visual tasks has led to significant progress in many domains. However, a key challenge remains: ensuring that models can generalize effectively to unseen samples or novel classes, especially in real-world scenarios where training data-target pairs are often limited or unavailable, and test data may exhibit shifts in both data and targets. This thesis addresses the problem of shifts across data and targets, proposing novel methods to improve model generalization and transferability in complex settings. The thesis identifies the different shift scenarios for visual tasks and presents their problem forms. The research first relaxes the static target distribution assumption in Multi-Domain Generalization (mDG) tasks, introducing the General Multi-Domain Generalization (GMDG) objective to improve generalization under varying data shifts. Specifically, Extensive experiments validate that GMDG is feasible for classification, segmentation, and regression tasks. Further considering extreme target distribution shifts where even unknown novel classes emerge, the study also explores logical regularization techniques for tasks such as Generalized Category Discovery (GCD), mDG+GCD, and Class Incremental Learning (CIL), proposing a sample-based logical regularization term (L-Reg) to enhance data-, target-, and all-shift generalization. Additionally, a partial logic framework is introduced to address challenges in CIL, enabling models to retain room for unknown classes during training. This is further extended by the Partial-Logic Regularization (PL-Reg), which improves generalization across GCD, mDG+GCD, and transferability for CIL tasks. Furthermore, the thesis proposes a novel Semantic-aware Data Augmentation (SADA) framework for cross-modality generalization in text-to-image synthesis (T2Isyn), text-image retrieval (TIR), and image-text retrieval (ITR) tasks. This framework ensures semantic preservation across text and image modalities, improving both semantic consistency and image quality in cross-modality tasks. The methods proposed in this thesis offer significant advancements in visual generalization and transfer scenarios, providing theoretical insights and practical solutions for handling data shifts, target shifts, and multi-modalities in complex scenarios. Extensive experiments validate the effectiveness of the proposed methods, demonstrating their superior performance across a range of tasks.

title: Depth of Processing, learner aptitude, and the acquisition of L2 English grammatical structures
authors: Shweta Nigam
abstract: Depth of Processing (DoP) is central to several models of instructed second language acquisition (ISLA) (Leow, 2015). While DoP has been extensively examined in vocabulary learning (e.g., Laufer & Hulstijn, 2001), its role in the acquisition of grammatical structures, particularly through oral and audio-visual modalities remains comparatively underexplored. Drawing on the Levels of Processing framework (Craik & Lockhart, 1972), this study investigated whether task-induced processing depth influences the acquisition of third conditionals and comparatives, and whether language aptitude (LLAMA B, D, F) predicts learning gains. Using a pretest–posttest design, four intact classes involving 108 Grade 8 EFL learners in India were assigned to one of the three experimental conditions differing in level and type of processing: Low DoP, High DoP Explicit, and High DoP Implicit. The treatment task required the participants to listen to an audio-visual story containing the target structures (third conditionals and comparatives) and complete analytic tasks (varying in different groups) before listening to the story for a second time. The oral performance of the participants was analysed for accuracy, and frequency of use of the target structures. A grammaticality judgement test (GJT) and an elicited imitation task (EIT) were used to assess the participants’ gains in the knowledge of the target structures. In addition, language aptitude (LLAMA B, D, F) was measured and modelled as a predictor of gain scores. Results showed a significant effect of processing condition on GJT performance with the High DoP Implicit group outperforming the High DoP Explicit group on total scores and comparatives. In contrast, ANCOVA analyses indicated no significant group differences on EIT outcomes once pretest performance was controlled, with pretest scores strongly predicting posttest performance. In oral production, processing effects were structure-specific: the Low DoP group showed greater accuracy gains for comparatives, while both High DoP groups revealed increased frequency of use of third conditionals. However, across all four measures, multiple regression analyses indicated that LLAMA B, D, and F did not significantly predict gain scores. Overall, the findings support a processing-by-structure pattern: deeper processing benefits were most evident for the more salient structure (comparatives) on an explicit, written measure, whereas complex, low-salience forms (third conditionals) showed limited accuracy change but increased frequency of use under deeper processing.

title: A UAV-Based Framework for Community-Scale Residential Building Energy Modelling in China
authors: Mengfan Jin
abstract: With increasing emphasis on energy efficiency and carbon emission reduction in the building sector, rapid and scalable energy modelling of existing buildings is critical for retrofit projects and policy development. Conventional surveys, data collection and energy modelling processes remain labour-intensive and impractical for large-scale applications, and energy modelling often dominates project time and cost. Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) equipped with high-resolution and infrared cameras now offer fast and safe exterior surveys, showing great potential in building energy assessments. Yet, a systematic framework for UAV integration, from image capture through processing to inputs for building energy simulation, has not been established. This research addresses these challenges by developing a structured framework for community-scale building energy modelling, which integrates UAV photogrammetry to accelerate data acquisition, reduce labour, and shorten energy modelling time for retrofit projects. The framework is designed to minimise prior data requirements while maximising automation and retaining sufficient accuracy and reliability. It also addressed systemic issues, such as the lack of data necessary to fully exploit the potential of available technologies in the context of this study. To achieve this research objective, a mixed-methodology approach, combining desk studies and fieldwork, was adopted. First, a comprehensive review of UAV-based building energy studies mapped the current applications and available tools, proposing a preliminary framework. Fieldwork then encompassed a pilot study and a detailed case study. In the pilot test, a single building was surveyed to identify an optimal toolchain for flight planning, image capture, photogrammetric reconstruction, model generation, and selection of a simulation platform. The resulting refined framework was applied to a case study of a 39-building community, and it was demonstrated that further automation was necessary. The potential for automation was then further explored. Geomatic algorithms, machine learning, and deep learning techniques were compared, and the combination that best balanced accuracy and processing time was selected for 3D model generation and window-to-wall ratio (WWR) extraction. In parallel, an archetype library of residential buildings in the Hot Summer Cold Winter (HSCW) zone in China was compiled to facilitate the assignment of thermal parameters. Finally, a reusable community-scale building energy modelling (CBEM) workflow was assembled in Grasshopper using Ladybug Tools components to process the aforementioned inputs. In conclusion, this study integrates UAV photogrammetry, GIS-based geomatic algorithms, machine learning, and graphical programming to develop an UAV-CBEM framework. The outcomes establish a foundation for scalable UAV-based building energy assessments, enhancing applicability in data-limited and large-scale settings worldwide.

title: Spectral Materialism: Encounters with land-time-scapes
authors: Nightingale, Sam
abstract: This transdisciplinary, practice-based PhD introduces spectral materialism through art-based research encounters with ecologically and historically stratified land-time-scapes shaped by hypersalinity and colonial terraforming. Centred in the semi-arid Mallee (southeastern Australia) and read through echoes with California’s Imperial Valley, the project examines how spectral time—the co-presence and haunting of other temporalities—manifests in the material conditions of salt, soil, water, plants, and infrastructures. It asks how learning from geological, First Nations, colonial, and ecological pasts can orient responsibilities in unsettled futures. Treating the present as a crisis of time as much as a crisis of matter, the thesis critiques linear-progressive temporalities bound to Western modernity and extractive regimes. In response, spectral materialism is developed as both a conceptual framework and a critical creative methodology. Through alchemical media experiments with salt crystals, hypersaline soils, and halophytes, photography is reconfigured as a site-responsive, process-oriented practice. Salt is engaged as a material agent and ‘time-crystal’ whose phase shifts—dissolution, saturation, precipitation, crystallisation, evaporation—form a meta-chemistry that refracts deep-marine pasts, settler-colonial irrigation infrastructures, and contemporary dust into processual renderings of time. Methodologically, the project advances attunement as a mode of sensing and responsiveness to forces that are not always immediately perceptible yet are materially active. Field notes appear as para-writing, interrupting linear narration so that heterogeneous times co-present themselves within the text. The thesis is guided by First Nations temporalities—time as relational and in place—while remaining accountable to ethical limits and protocols. The contribution is twofold: a theoretical articulation of spectral materialism as a way to think time otherwise, and a set of site-responsive methods for engaging elemental media in saline environments. Together, they generate materially grounded accounts of spectral presences and open alternative pathways for knowing, sensing, and relating within land-time-scapes marked by enduring colonial and ecological afterlives amid planetary change.

title: DEVELOPMENT AND COMMERCIALIZATION OF COMPUTATIONAL METHODS TO ACCELERATE DERMATOLOGICAL DISCOVERY
authors: Jasson Makkar
abstract: The skin is the largest and outermost organ that surrounds the human body and provides a physical barrier that protects the more delicate internal tissues from the harsh surrounding environment. Over the course of evolution, specialized structures have also arisen in the skin, including sweat and sebaceous glands, nails and claws, and hair follicles. The hair follicle is a multi-lineage mini-organ that is a critical component in defining mammalian species. The gain of function derived from hair and fur benefited these species for millennia due to its insulative and protective properties, mechanosensing function, and ability to serve as camouflage. Current approaches to assess these fibers are generally non-quantitative or are low throughput due to technical limitations of ‘splitting hairs’. We developed a novel deep learning-based computer vision approach for the high throughput quantification of individual hair fibers at a high resolution. Our innovative computer vision tool can distinguish and extract overlapping fibers for quantification of multivariate features including length, width, and color to generate single-hair phenomes (shPhenome) of diverse conditions across the lifespan of mice. Using our tool, we explored the effects of hormone signaling, genetic modifications, and aging on hair follicle output. These analyses revealed novel hair phenotypes as a result of endocrinological, developmental, and aging-related alterations in the fur coats of mice. This tool was then adapted to capture more nuanced hair phenotypes, such as curvature, in a variety of mouse models harboring genetic perturbations. Commercialization of the deep hair phenomics technology presented a unique opportunity to pursue research translation, transforming fundamental biological research into marketable products. Much like the traditional academic route, the path to commercialization requires consistent and continuous iteration, testing of hypotheses, and allowing data to influence and lead subsequent actions. However, as opposed to the pursuit of knowledge, translating research into market-ready solutions requires a focus on consumer needs and the identification of market opportunities. Additionally, the shift in incentive structure requires commercial ventures to prioritize intellectual property protection, alter capital and resource allocation, and seek alternative fundraising sources. The entrepreneurial foundation built through this process culminated in the filing of a provisional patent and establishment of a startup company, kerat Inc. This journey illuminated the multifaceted challenges inherent in closing the gap between academic innovation and commercially viable goods, requiring simultaneous advancement of technical capabilities, adaptation to market dynamics, and fabrication of business infrastructure. Overall, the culmination of work presented in this dissertation sheds light on the importance of quantitatively assessing hair fiber properties to capture the biological phenomena that underlie this fundamental feature of mammalian skin. These findings also highlight the capabilities of this methodology for identifying perturbations in normal growth, potentially indicative of disease or dysfunction. Lastly, this showcased the potential of this technology’s commercial use cases in both the cosmetics and diagnostics industries.

title: Contested urbanisms: The politics of heritage and housing in Jakarta’s kampungs
authors: Binte Masron, Irna Nurlina
abstract: Do heritage-making projects resist or advance gentrification in Southeast Asia? Like other Global South cities, contested urbanisms chequer Jakarta’s postcolonial urban landscape. Competing ideas about urban development manifest in various ways of seeing and producing the city, as demonstrated by evictions, revitalisation projects, and informal housing. Increased evictions of urban villages (urban kampungs) between 2013 and 2018 in Jakarta saw growing grassroots heritage movements as part of a spectrum of resistance to top-down urban management by state and private sector actors who also stake their claims on what ‘heritage’ is. These tensions amongst the political projects of various actors led me to ask: how do heritage-making projects of/by urban villages affect housing conditions in Jakarta, with reference to gentrification-led displacement? Using ethnographic methods and thematic analysis, I delve into the constructions of heritage, the impact of heritage-making on housing security for residents, and the broader political impact of heritage-making from above and below in Jakarta’s Kota Tua and two of its kampungs, Luar Batang and Pekojan. I argue that the dominant heritage constructions in Kota Tua demonstrate a top-down logic that emphasises infrastructure and the built environment with strong private sector presence, which impact the kampungs in varied ways. Findings showed that top-down heritage-making demonstrates higher likelihood of driving gentrification through the commodification of space, prioritising capital and material values. Residents and their advocates employ heritage-making from below in various forms to reclaim their place in the city as they face various forms of displacement, with unanticipated consequences. The processes of heritage-making from above and below reveal the connections and disjunctures between different authorities which subaltern actors work through, producing new politics that contest or entrench existing conditions. The findings contribute to the theorising of the politics of gentrification in heritage and urban studies, and a deeper understanding of Jakarta’s Old Town.

title: From Sparse to Dense: Label-Efficient Weakly Supervised Segmentation for Images and Videos
authors: Wang, Jian
abstract: Obtaining high-quality annotated data has become a primary bottleneck for training deep learning models, particularly for dense prediction tasks like semantic segmentation and video salient object segmentation. The demand for meticulous, pixel-level labeling makes fully-supervised approaches prohibitively expensive and limits their scalability. This thesis directly confronts this issue by proposing and systematically investigating a label-efficient "sparse-to-dense'' paradigm. The core objective is to develop innovative frameworks that can learn from sparse, inexpensive weak supervision—such as image-level tags or scribbles—and intelligently propagate this minimal information to generate complete, pixel-accurate dense predictions. The major part of this thesis focuses on the "sparse-to-dense'' challenge within Weakly Supervised Semantic Segmentation (WSSS) for images, where models learn from only image-level tags. Dominant approaches rely on Class Activation Maps (CAMs) as initial object seeds. However, CAMs inherently activate only the most discriminative object regions, leading to incomplete pseudo-labels. This gives rise to the central problem of activation densification: the critical process of expanding these sparse activations to cover the full extent of an object. Our research addresses this challenge through a progressive, multi-faceted strategy. Our exploration begins with a foundational framework (C3) designed to rectify the intrinsic flaws of initial CAMs. We propose a synergistic mutual calibration method. This method leverages the discrepancies between the two maps to generate local prototypes, which are simultaneously utilized to complete missing object parts and suppress background noise, yielding a significantly more accurate and complete initial seed. This foundational work immediately reveals the limitation of single-prototype instability and its inability to capture diverse features. Building on this foundation, we then develop architecture-specific strategies to address deeper limitations of the prototype-based approach. For Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) (C4), the use of a single prototype proves insufficient to capture significant intra-class variation. In response, we introduce an Optimal Transport (OT)-assisted framework that effectively mines multiple, diverse prototypes, thereby yielding more comprehensive activation maps. However, while C4 solves the intra-class diversity problem, the inherent local context constraint of the CNN architecture becomes the new bottleneck, fundamentally limiting the quality of globally-aware feature extraction needed for optimal multi-prototype assignment. This limitation necessitates a shift in architectural focus from CNNs to Vision Transformers. In the ViT architecture (C5), a new challenge arises where the token gap between the discriminative class token and varied patch tokens leads to incomplete activation. To bridge this gap, we leverage a tailored application of Optimal Transport, where the algorithm is tasked with learning a comprehensive proxy to ensure complete object activation. Despite these architectural advances (C3-C5), the overall WSSS performance hit a ceiling. This is fundamentally limited by the sparse supervision of class labels, which cannot provide precise boundary information. To break this ceiling, our WSSS exploration culminates in a universal enhancement strategy (C6) that transcends architecture-specific designs by leveraging Visual Foundation Models (VFMs). We resolve the conflict between the discriminative nature of initial CAMs and the VFM's need for holistic prompts. By modeling the CAM foreground as a graph and employing spectral analysis, our method intelligently selects a diverse set of prompt points that represent the overall structure of the foreground object. This guides the VFM to generate superior, boundary-aware supervision that can universally enhance any WSSS pipeline. Subsequently, the thesis extends the "sparse-to-dense'' paradigm to the dynamic domain of video, addressing Weakly Supervised Video Salient Object Segmentation (WSVSOS) (C7) from sparse scribble annotations. In this specific context, the challenge evolves into spatio-temporal densification, which requires both full-object coverage within each frame and temporal consistency across the video sequences. To this end, we introduce the core CFMR framework, which utilizes Spatio-Temporal co-regulation. This framework is subsequently enhanced (CFMR+) by integrating the VFM guidance strategy from C6, which provides high-quality spatial priors essential for ensuring both high spatial detail and inter-frame consistency. By enforcing both intra-frame and cross-frame consistency between these two streams, our method effectively propagates the sparse initial signal to generate dense and temporally coherent saliency masks. In conclusion, this thesis presents a comprehensive and cohesive investigation into label-efficient segmentation tasks, offering a suite of innovative and effective strategies for the "sparse-to-dense'' challenge. Our work establishes a progressive roadmap that systematically overcomes architectural and semantic limitations, culminating in highly robust and generalized densification pipelines. Our extensive experimental results on standard benchmarks validate the state-of-the-art performance of these methods, providing robust solutions to a long-standing problem in the computer vision field.

title: Unsupervised Deep-learning Methods for Low-dose Computed Tomography Reconstruction
authors: An, Ran
abstract: Computed tomography (CT) has become an indispensable imaging technique in medical diagnostics and industrial applications, owing to its non-invasive nature and high resolution in visualizing object internal structures. While X-ray CT (X-ray computed tomography) significantly enhances lesion detection capabilities, excessive exposure to X-ray radiation raises substantial health concerns, including elevated cancer risks and potential genetic damage. Although low-dose CT (LDCT) protocols reduce radiation safety concerns, they inevitably introduce severe noise and artifacts, which might compromise diagnostic accuracy. Recent advances in supervised deep learning approaches have demonstrated remarkable success in LDCT reconstruction. However, the reliance on paired training data severely limits their deployment in practical CT applications. This fundamental constraint highlights the critical importance of developing unsupervised reconstruction methods. Although existing unsupervised LDCT methods have made notable progress, they still face challenges requiring systematic solutions. This thesis makes three contributions to advance the field of unsupervised LDCT reconstruction: 1. Current dual-domain self-supervised LDCT denoising methods typically neglect the heterogeneity of the non-stationary Gaussian noise levels in low-dose sinograms and usually treat them as common images without appropriately controlling the denoising strength. The denoisers employed by them, which are based on classic convolutional neural networks (CNN), will lead to blurring artifacts in the reconstructed images if directly used for sinogram denoising. In addition, the denoising strength in the sinogram and image domains must be well-balanced to avoid introducing over-blurring or secondary artifacts in the reconstructed images, but existing approaches do not focus on this crucial point. To address these limitations, this thesis proposes a novel end-to-end dual-domain self-supervised framework for LDCT denoising. It employs Dropblock layers to adaptively localize the effect of convolution for sinogram denoising and sets a weighted average between the denoised sinograms and their noisy counterparts to better control the denoising strength, thus effectively reducing the blurring artifacts and leading to a well-balanced dual-domain denoising. Numerical experiments demonstrate the effectiveness and superior performance of the proposed method. 2. Existing normalizing flows (NFs)-based unsupervised LDCT reconstruction methods face challenges in both image quality and computational efficiency. On one hand, they typically utilize a two-way transformation strategy between noisy images and latent variables, which could easily lead to detail loss and secondary artifacts in the reconstructed images. On the other hand, training NFs on high-resolution CT images is computationally intensive. Although conditional normalizing flows (CNFs) can mitigate computational costs by learning conditional probabilities, existing approaches rely on labeled data for conditionalization, leaving unsupervised CNFs-based LDCT reconstruction a challenge. To tackle these issues, this thesis proposes a novel unsupervised LDCT iterative reconstruction algorithm based on CNFs. The proposed method employs a strict one-way transformation strategy during the alternating optimization in the dual spaces to prevent detail loss and secondary artifacts, and proposes a novel unsupervised conditionalization strategy for CNFs, thus achieving efficient training and inference on high-resolution images. The proposed method illustrates high-quality and relatively fast unsupervised reconstruction. Experiments across two datasets demonstrate the superior performance of the proposed method by rivaling several state-of-the-art methods. 3. Current diffusion model-based LDCT reconstruction methods solely employ the prior distributions learned from normal-dose CT data but neglect the valuable priors in low-dose data, which contain information about the characteristics of low-dose noise and artifacts. In addition, their reconstruction speed suffers from multiple sampling steps, presenting low efficiency. Breaking new ground in prior utilization, this thesis proposes a novel unsupervised LDCT iterative reconstruction algorithm based on dual denoising diffusion probabilistic models (DDPM), which leverages both normal-dose and low-dose priors. Specifically, the proposed method employs two DDPMs to learn the prior distributions from normal-dose and low-dose images, respectively, and incorporates them into a joint iterative reconstruction framework. To accelerate the reconstruction, partial diffusion sampling and single-pass deterministic reconstruction strategy are utilized in the proposed method, as well as the spaced OS-SART approaches. Experiments at different dose levels demonstrate the outstanding performance and fast speed of the proposed reconstruction algorithm. Through these innovations and contributions, this thesis addresses some significant challenges in current deep-learning-based unsupervised LDCT reconstruction methods, and proposes three novel unsupervised reconstruction algorithms. The proposed methods effectively improve the performance and efficiency of LDCT reconstruction under different unsupervised learning conditions, and provide some new perspectives and inspirations for future research.

title: Data and code for: Deep learning reveals distinct and complementary cis-regulatory grammar from STARR-seq and lentiMPRA
authors: Ji Yun; Ville Tiusanen; Konsta Karttunen; Divyesh Patel; Esa Pitkänen; Biswajyoti Sahu
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Overview This record accompanies the manuscript "Deep learning reveals distinct and complementary cis-regulatory grammar from STARR-seq and lentiMPRA". The archive contains processed data, analysis workflows, selected model artifacts, source records, and figure-level outputs used to compare episomal genomic STARR-seq and integrated lentivirus-based MPRA in HepG2 cells. The study integrates assay signal comparison, cCRE and epigenomic annotation, transcription factor ChIP-seq correlation, motif enrichment, regression-based motif activity analysis, and sequence-based deep learning to characterize shared and assay-specific cis-regulatory grammar. Contents This release includes: processed STARR-seq and lentiMPRA analysis inputs; DeepSTARR FASTA/TSV model input files; lentiMPRA probe-level and STARR-seq peak-level activity tables; selected raw/source files redistributed with the release; public accession tables and source-resource inventories; JASPAR 2024 motif files and transcription factor annotation tables; workflow scripts for data preparation, signal comparison, motif analysis, model training and evaluation, and supplementary analyses; MEIRLOP and GimmeMotifs result tables and figure outputs; trained DeepSTARR baseline model files, held-out test splits, predictions, and performance summaries; manuscript figures and supplementary outputs; environment/version notes; MANIFEST.tsv and checksums.tsv for file inventory and SHA256 verification. Workflow Modules The release is organized into the following workflow modules: 01_data_preparation 02_signal_comparison 03_chip_epigenome_correlation 04_meirlop 05_gimmemotifs 06_deepstarr 07_supplementary_features MPRALegnet.tar.gz Each module contains the scripts, intermediate outputs, and documentation required to reproduce the corresponding analyses. Scope and External Inputs This archive provides a reproducible snapshot of the computational analyses performed for the manuscript. Original public datasets are not redistributed and should be downloaded from their respective repositories using the accession tables and references provided in the manuscript and accompanying source files. Large third-party resources, including the GRCh38 reference genome and selected ENCODE ChIP-seq and epigenomic bigWig files, are documented but not bundled. Their expected locations and regeneration instructions are described in the workflow README files. This release includes DeepSTARR model artifacts. MPRALegNet training, attribution analyses, TF-MoDISco results, and associated model files are documented as deferred components and are not included in this release. Licensing Code is released under the MIT License. Project-generated documentation and data tables are released under CC BY 4.0, subject to the licenses of the original public data providers.
